title: Design a rate limiter, auth service and classics
seriesDescription: Topic-by-topic JEE-style quizzes for the backend and AI-engineering interview roadmap: integer, assertion-reason, matrix match, fill-in-the-blanks, short code writing, plus multi-correct questions. Language core, concurrency, DSA, web frameworks, data access, databases, messaging, resilience, security, testing, system design, LLM and agent engineering.
description: Rate limiter algorithms and numbers, a JWT authentication service with JWKS, and the classic interview designs: URL shortener, news feed, chat, notifications, search autocomplete and distributed cache.
source: Stripe and Cloudflare rate limiting write-ups; System Design Interview (Xu); Hello Interview and Educative problem lists; RFC 7517 (JWKS); Redis docs; Karger et al. consistent hashing

questions.prompt: A token bucket has capacity 10 and refills 5 tokens per second. It starts full, and 30 requests arrive at the same instant (each needs one token). How many are allowed?
questions.explanation: The bucket can hand out only the 10 tokens it holds. The refill adds nothing within a single instant, so 20 requests are rejected with 429.

questions.prompt: A sliding-window-counter limiter keeps counts per fixed minute. The previous minute had 80 requests, the current minute has 30 so far, and we are 25% into the current minute. What is the weighted estimate of requests in the last 60 seconds?
questions.explanation: Estimate = previous x (1 - 0.25) + current = 80 x 0.75 + 30 = 90. It approximates a true sliding log using only two counters per key.

questions.prompt: A fixed-window limiter allows 100 requests per minute per user. What is the largest number of requests that can be accepted in a 2-second span straddling a window boundary?
questions.explanation: 100 at the end of one window and 100 at the start of the next: 200 in about 2 seconds. This burst problem motivates sliding windows and token buckets.

questions.prompt: Match each rate-limiting algorithm to its key property.

right.text: Allows bursts up to the bucket size, then limits the average rate
Smooths output to a constant rate via a queue
Simplest, but allows a double burst at window boundaries
Exact, but stores a timestamp per request
Approximate, using two counters and a weight
Blocks all clients when the load average is high

questions.explanation: Pick token bucket for API quotas with bursts, leaky bucket when downstream needs a steady rate.

questions.prompt: Write the two redis-cli commands that implement a fixed-window counter for user u42 in minute window 28500123: increment the key rl:u42:28500123 and make it expire after 60 seconds.
questions.explanation: In production use a Lua script or MULTI so INCR and EXPIRE are atomic (otherwise a crash between them leaves a key that never expires), and SET NX EX 60 followed by INCR also works.

questions.prompt: Complete the HTTP behaviour of a rate limiter.
questions.text: A gateway that rejects an over-limit client returns status {1} and a {2} header that tells the client when to try again, and it usually identifies the caller by API key or {3}.
questions.explanation: Many APIs also return X-RateLimit-Limit and X-RateLimit-Remaining headers; the IETF RateLimit header fields are a draft standard.

questions.prompt: Read the assertion and the reason, then choose the option that describes them correctly.
questions.assertion: A rate limiter running on many API servers usually keeps its counters in a shared store such as Redis.
questions.reason: Redis operations such as INCR are atomic.

whys.a: Right: atomic increments avoid lost updates across servers.
whys.b: The atomicity is a main reason the shared store works.

questions.explanation: Per-node local limits are cheaper but let total traffic exceed the global limit by the number of nodes.

questions.prompt: In a JWT-based authentication service, how should the many downstream services verify tokens?

options.text: Fetch and cache the public keys from the auth service's JWKS endpoint
options.why: Right: verification is local, and the auth service is off the hot path.

options.text: Call the auth service on every request to introspect the token
options.why: It works but makes the auth service a bottleneck and a single point of failure.

options.text: Share the private signing key with every service
options.why: Any service holding it could mint tokens.

options.text: Trust the user id sent in a plain header
options.why: Anyone can set a header, so no verification would exist.

questions.explanation: Use RS256 or ES256 with kid, rotate keys by publishing the new key before signing with it, and keep access TTLs short with refresh tokens.

questions.prompt: Read the assertion and the reason, then choose the option that describes them correctly.
questions.assertion: An auth service should publish public keys through JWKS and identify each with a kid.
questions.reason: This lets keys be rotated without downtime.

whys.a: Right: old and new keys are listed together, and verifiers pick by kid.
whys.b: The reason is the purpose of kid.

questions.explanation: During rotation, publish the new key, switch signing, then retire the old key after the longest token TTL.

questions.prompt: A URL shortener must be able to encode 100 billion distinct URLs with base62 codes (a-z, A-Z, 0-9). What is the minimum code length?
questions.explanation: 62^6 is about 56.8 billion, which is too small. 62^7 is about 3.5 trillion, so 7 characters suffice.

questions.prompt: A chat service expects 10 million concurrent WebSocket connections, and one gateway server can hold 100,000 connections. How many gateway servers are needed at minimum?
questions.explanation: 10,000,000 / 100,000 = 100. In practice you add headroom and spread across zones, so a design would say about 120 to 150.

questions.prompt: In a news feed, ordinary users have a few hundred followers but celebrities have millions. What is the standard design answer?

options.text: Hybrid: fan-out on write for normal users, on-read merge for celebrities
options.why: Right: it avoids millions of writes per celebrity post while keeping normal feeds fast.

options.text: Fan-out on write for everyone, including celebrities
options.why: One celebrity post would trigger millions of writes.

options.text: Compute every feed on read by scanning all followed users
options.why: It makes the read path slow for users who follow many accounts.

options.text: Store only the post and email followers a link
options.why: It does not provide a feed at all.

questions.explanation: Push gives fast reads and costly writes, pull gives cheap writes and slow reads. Real systems mix them.

questions.prompt: Match each classic design problem to its signature component or technique.

right.text: Unique id generator plus base62 encoding
Fan-out service and per-user timeline cache
WebSocket gateways with a per-conversation sequence number
Queue per channel with retries, dedupe and provider workers
Trie or prefix index with precomputed top-k suggestions
Consistent hashing to route keys to nodes

questions.explanation: In the interview, name the signature component and then spend the deep dive on its failure mode.

questions.prompt: Read the assertion and the reason, then choose the option that describes them correctly.
questions.assertion: Consistent hashing minimises key movement when a cache node is added.
questions.reason: With key mod N placement, adding a node moves only about 1/N of the keys.

whys.c: Right: with modulo placement most keys change nodes when N changes, which is why consistent hashing is used.
whys.d: The assertion is the true statement.

questions.explanation: Consistent hashing moves roughly 1/(N+1) of the keys; virtual nodes even out the load.

questions.prompt: Read the assertion and the reason, then choose the option that describes them correctly.
questions.assertion: A notification system should call the push and SMS providers directly from the API request thread to be reliable.
questions.reason: Providers such as APNs, FCM and SMS gateways are slow and rate limited.

whys.d: Right: the reason is true, and it is exactly why work should go through a queue with retries instead.

questions.explanation: Accept the request, persist it, enqueue per channel, and let workers retry with backoff and an idempotency key.

questions.prompt: Read the assertion and the reason, then choose the option that describes them correctly.
questions.assertion: Messages in a conversation need a per-conversation sequence number.

whys.b: Right: both are true but unrelated; ordering comes from the sequence, not the transport.

questions.explanation: Server clocks drift, so sequence numbers (or a per-conversation log) give a stable order and let clients detect gaps.
